<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A configuration
\[
\Lambda=(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\subset\mathbb R^p
\]
is \emph{admissible} if the following conditions hold:
\[
0\in\operatorname{conv}\{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\},
\]
and
\[
0\in\operatorname{conv}\{\lambda_i:i\in I\}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|I|>p.
\]
The first condition is the Siegel condition and the second is weak
hyperbolicity.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:smooth}
If $\Lambda$ is admissible, then
$Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ is a compact smooth manifold of dimension
\[
4n-p-1=4n-4m-1.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Consider
\[
F:\mathbb H^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R,
\qquad
F(q)=
\left(
\sum_i\lambda_i|q_i|^2,\,
\sum_i|q_i|^2
\right).
\]
Then
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)=F^{-1}(0,1).
\]
For $q\in Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ let
\[
I(q)=\{i:q_i\neq0\}.
\]
The differential is
\[
dF_q(h)
=
2\left(
\sum_i\lambda_i\operatorname{Re}(\overline q_i h_i),\,
\sum_i\operatorname{Re}(\overline q_i h_i)
\right).
\]
For $i\in I(q)$ the real number
$\operatorname{Re}(\overline q_i h_i)$ can be prescribed arbitrarily by
taking $h_i$ proportional to $q_i$.  Thus $dF_q$ is onto if and only if
the augmented vectors
\[
\{\widetilde\lambda_i:i\in I(q)\}
\]
span $\mathbb R^{p+1}$.

Since
\[
0=\sum_{i\in I(q)}|q_i|^2\lambda_i,\qquad
1=\sum_{i\in I(q)}|q_i|^2,
\]
the origin belongs to the convex hull of the vectors in the support.
If their affine span had dimension at most $p-1$, Carath\'eodory's theorem
in that affine span would place the origin in the convex hull of at most
$p$ of them.  This contradicts weak hyperbolicity.  Hence the augmented
vectors have rank $p+1$.

Thus $(0,1)$ is a regular value of $F$.  Compactness follows from the sphere
equation and the dimension is
\[
4n-(p+1).
\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:support}
Every point of $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ has at least $4m+1$ nonzero coordinates.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:polytope}
The map
\[
\mu(q)=\bigl(|q_1|^2,\ldots,|q_n|^2\bigr)
\]
has image $P_\Lambda$, and its fibres are exactly the
$\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n$ orbits.  Hence
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)/\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n\cong P_\Lambda.
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Only the statement about the fibres needs proof.  If $\mu(q)=\mu(q')$, then
$|q_i|=|q_i'|$ for every $i$.  For a nonzero coordinate there is a unit
quaternion $u_i$ such that $q_i'=q_i u_i$.  When $q_i=0$ the corresponding
factor is arbitrary.  Therefore $q$ and $q'$ lie in the same orbit.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:faces}
The set $F_J$ is nonempty if and only if
$0\in\operatorname{conv}\{\lambda_i:i\notin J\}$. In that case $F_J$ contains a
point with $x_i>0$ for every $i\notin J$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
A point of $F_J$ gives a convex representation of $0$ by the weights
with indices outside $J$, and conversely. If $0$ lies in this convex
hull, the supporting-hyperplane argument above, using weak
hyperbolicity, puts $0$ in its interior. Averaging as above gives a
convex representation with all coefficients $x_i$, $i\notin J$,
strictly positive.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:simple}
The polytope $P_\Lambda$ is simple.  Indispensable coordinates correspond
to inequalities $x_i\ge0$ which never become active; they do not create
additional facets.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $x$ be a vertex and let $I=\{i:x_i>0\}$ be its support.  If
$|I|>p+1$, the augmented columns $(\lambda_i,1)$, $i\in I$, are linearly
dependent.  A nonzero relation among them gives a nontrivial tangent
direction inside the coordinate face determined by the support of $x$,
contradicting that $x$ is a vertex.  Hence $|I|\le p+1$.  On the other hand, the defining equations give
$0\in\operatorname{conv}\{\lambda_i:i\in I\}$, so weak hyperbolicity gives
$|I|>p$.  Hence $|I|=p+1$.

The augmented columns $(\lambda_i,1)$, $i\in I$, are linearly independent:
otherwise the vertex would be degenerate, equivalently there would be a
nonzero tangent direction supported in $I$.

Let
\[
T=\{h\in\mathbb R^n:\textstyle\sum_i\lambda_ih_i=0,\ \sum_ih_i=0\}
\]
be the tangent space to the affine slice defining $P_\Lambda$; it does not
depend on the base point and has dimension $d=n-p-1$.  Independence of
$\{(\lambda_i,1):i\in I\}$ says precisely that $T\cap\mathbb R^I=0$, where
$\mathbb R^I\subset\mathbb R^n$ is the coordinate subspace supported on $I$.  Since
$\dim T=d=|[n]\setminus I|$, this forces the projection
$T\to\mathbb R^{[n]\setminus I}$, $h\mapsto(h_j)_{j\notin I}$, to be a linear
isomorphism, which is exactly the asserted independence of the restrictions
$x_j|_T$, $j\notin I$.  Thus the $d=n-p-1$
coordinate hyperplanes $x_j=0$, $j\notin I$, have independent restrictions
to the affine space defining $P_\Lambda$.  Each is therefore a facet near
$x$, and exactly $d$ facets meet at $x$.  Since $x$ was arbitrary,
$P_\Lambda$ is simple.  If $i$ is indispensable, then $x_i>0$ everywhere,
so $x_i=0$ is not among the facets.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:real-commuting}
For all $U,V\in\mathbb R^{4m}$,
\[
[X_U,X_V]=0.
\]
Consequently the distribution tangent to the canonical real dilation
orbits is involutive on every constant-rank stratum.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The coefficients $\langle\lambda_i,U\rangle$ and
$\langle\lambda_i,V\rangle$ are real constants.  On the $i$th
quaternionic coordinate both vector fields are therefore scalar radial
fields, and their linear endomorphisms commute.  Hence their Lie bracket
vanishes coordinate by coordinate.  Equivalently, these vector fields
are the infinitesimal generators of the abelian action
$\mathbb R^{4m}\curvearrowright\mathbb H^n$ used below.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:hessian}
One has
\[
\nabla f_q(T)=
2\sum_i|q_i|^2e^{2\langle\lambda_i,T\rangle}\lambda_i
\]
and
\[
D^2f_q(T)(X,X)
=
4\sum_i|q_i|^2e^{2\langle\lambda_i,T\rangle}
\langle\lambda_i,X\rangle^2.
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:interior}
If $\Lambda$ is admissible and $q\in\mathcal S_\Lambda$, then
\[
0\in\operatorname{int}
\operatorname{conv}\{\lambda_i:q_i\neq0\}
\]
in $\mathbb R^p$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If the origin lay on the boundary, a supporting face through the origin would
be contained in an affine hyperplane of dimension at most $p-1$.
Carath\'eodory's theorem in this hyperplane would express the origin as a
convex combination of at most $p$ vectors, contradicting weak hyperbolicity.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:proper}
For $q\in\mathcal S_\Lambda$, the function $f_q$ is strictly convex and proper.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Strict convexity follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:hessian}, because the support
spans $\mathbb R^p$.  For properness, Lemma~\ref{lem:interior} implies that in
every direction $X$ on the unit sphere some scalar product
$\langle\lambda_i,X\rangle$ is positive.  By compactness of the unit sphere,
the maximum of these positive scalar products is uniformly bounded away from
zero.  Hence along every sequence $|T|\to\infty$ at least one exponential
term tends to infinity.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:transversal}
Every $\mathbb R^p$ orbit in $\mathcal S_\Lambda$ contains a unique point of minimum
Euclidean norm.  At the minimum,
\[
\sum_i\lambda_i|q_i|^2=0.
\]
The map
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\times\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R_{>0}
\longrightarrow \mathcal S_\Lambda,
\qquad
(q,T,r)\longmapsto r\,\Phi_T(q),
\]
is a diffeomorphism.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Existence and uniqueness of the minimum follow from strict convexity and
properness.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:interior} the weights in the support of
$q$ span $\mathbb R^p$, so $\Phi_T(q)=q$ forces $\langle\lambda_i,T\rangle=0$ for all
$i$ in the support, hence $T=0$, and the action is free on
$\mathcal S_\Lambda$;
hence $T$ is determined by the point $r\Phi_T(q)$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:hessian}, the critical point equation is the
first defining equation of $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$.  Normalization gives the
sphere equation.  Smooth dependence on the initial point follows from the
implicit function theorem, since the Hessian at the critical point is
positive definite.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:projective}
The $\mathbb R^{4m}$ action descends to $V_\Lambda$ and
\[
V_\Lambda\cong N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\times\mathbb R^{4m}.
\]
In particular
\[
V_\Lambda/\mathbb R^{4m}\cong N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda).
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The action by real positive coordinate dilations commutes with positive
homotheties and with diagonal left multiplication by $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:transversal} and divide by these two actions.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:isotropy}
Let $[q]\in N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ and
\[
J(q)=\{i:q_i=0\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{Stab}_{\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n}([q])
\cong
\operatorname{Sp}(1)\times\operatorname{Sp}(1)^{|J(q)|}.
\]
In particular the principal isotropy group is $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The class $[q]$ is fixed by $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ precisely when there is
an $a\in\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ such that
\[
q_i u_i=a q_i
\]
for all $i$.  If $q_i\neq0$, then
\[
u_i=q_i^{-1}a q_i.
\]
If $q_i=0$, the element $u_i$ is arbitrary.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:polyprod}
There is an $\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n$-equivariant homeomorphism
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\cong(D^4,\mathbb S^{3})^{K_P},
\]
where an indispensable coordinate is represented by a ghost vertex of
$K_P$ and hence contributes an $\mathbb S^{3}$ factor.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:polytope}, the norm-square map is the orbit map and
there is a canonical model
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\cong(\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n\times P)/\!\sim,
\]
where $(u,x)\sim(u',x)$ precisely when $u_i=u_i'$ for every coordinate
with $x_i>0$; equivalently the $i$th $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ factor is collapsed on the
facet $x_i=0$.  Since $P$ is simple by Proposition~\ref{prop:simple}, its
facet nerve is $K_P$.  The standard polyhedral-product model for a simple
polytope identifies
\[
(\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n\times P)/\!\sim
\quad\text{with}\quad
(D^4,\mathbb S^{3})^{K_P};
\]
see, for example, \cite{BP,BBCG}.  Concretely, polar coordinates
$z_i=\rho_i u_i$ identify the radial variables with a cubical
neighborhood of the face lattice of $P$, while the phase $u_i$ becomes
irrelevant exactly when $\rho_i=0$, which is exactly the above
 equivalence relation.  These local identifications agree on face
intersections and are $\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n$-equivariant. They leave the phase
coordinates unchanged and therefore also commute with the diagonal
left $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ action.

If coordinate $i$ is indispensable, the facet $x_i=0$ is absent.  In the
simplicial description this is a ghost vertex, so the $i$th coordinate of
the polyhedral product is constrained to $\mathbb S^{3}$ everywhere and splits off
as an $\mathbb S^{3}$ factor.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:2connZ}
The manifold $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ is $2$-connected.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Use the CW structures with one $0$-cell and one $3$-cell on $\mathbb S^{3}$, and
with $\mathbb S^{3}$ as the boundary subcomplex of the $4$-cell $D^4$.  The induced
CW structure on $(D^4,\mathbb S^{3})^{K_P}$ has one $0$-cell and no cells of
dimension $1$ or $2$: every positive-dimensional cell has dimension at
least $3$.  By cellular approximation every map $\mathbb S^j\to Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$,
$j=1,2$, is homotopic into the $j$-skeleton, which is a point.  Thus
$\pi_1=\pi_2=0$.  Extra indispensable coordinates only add $\mathbb S^{3}$ factors
and do not change this conclusion.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:hochster}
There are natural additive decompositions
\[
\widetilde H^q(Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda);\mathbb Z)
\cong
\bigoplus_{\varnothing\ne J\subset[n]}
\widetilde H^{\,q-3|J|-1}((K_P)_J;\mathbb Z)
\]
and
\[
\widetilde H_q(Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda);\mathbb Z)
\cong
\bigoplus_{\varnothing\ne J\subset[n]}
\widetilde H_{\,q-3|J|-1}((K_P)_J;\mathbb Z).
\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
This is the $(D^4,\mathbb S^{3})$ specialization of the standard stable splitting
and cellular decomposition for polyhedral products; see
\cite{BBCG,BP}.  In the stable splitting, a subset $J$ contributes a
suspension shift of $3|J|+1$, which gives the displayed degree
$q-3|J|-1$ after taking reduced (co)homology.  The construction is
integral and cellular, so it yields the homology and cohomology
statements simultaneously.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:stablepar}
The manifold $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ is stably parallelizable:
\[
TZ_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\oplus\mathbb R^{4m+1}
\cong\mathbb R^{4n}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The $4m+1$ gradients of the defining equations give a global framing of the
normal bundle of $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ in $\mathbb H^n\simeq\mathbb R^{4n}$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:2connN}
Every LVMQ manifold is $2$-connected.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Use the homotopy exact sequence and
Corollary~\ref{cor:2connZ}, together with
\[
\pi_1(\mathbb S^{3})=\pi_2(\mathbb S^{3})=0.
\]
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:H4}
Assume that $\Lambda$ has no indispensable coordinates.  Then
$N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ is $3$-connected and
\[
H^4(N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z.
\]
The Euler class
\[
e\in H^4(N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda);\mathbb Z)
\]
of the principal $\mathbb S^{3}$ bundle is a generator.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:hochster}, in the absence of indispensable coordinates,
\[
H_3(Z_{\mathbb H};\mathbb Z)=0,
\qquad
H^3(Z_{\mathbb H};\mathbb Z)=H^4(Z_{\mathbb H};\mathbb Z)=0.
\]
For $|J|=1$, the full subcomplex $K_J$ is a simplex, since there are
no ghost vertices. For $|J|\ge2$ and $q=3,4$, the degree
$q-3|J|-1$ in the generalized Hochster formula is less than $-1$.
Thus all the relevant summands vanish.

Since $Z_{\mathbb H}$ is $2$-connected, the Hurewicz homomorphism
$\pi_3(Z_{\mathbb H})\to H_3(Z_{\mathbb H};\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism.  Hence
$\pi_3(Z_{\mathbb H})=0$.  The homotopy exact sequence of the principal $\mathbb S^{3}$
bundle then gives
\[
\pi_3(N_{\mathbb H})=0.
\]
Thus $N_{\mathbb H}$ is $3$-connected.

The Gysin sequence contains
\[
H^3(Z_{\mathbb H})
\longrightarrow H^0(N_{\mathbb H})
\stackrel{\smile e}{\longrightarrow}
H^4(N_{\mathbb H})
\longrightarrow H^4(Z_{\mathbb H}).
\]
The two outer groups vanish, so multiplication by $e$ identifies
$H^0(N_{\mathbb H})\cong\mathbb Z$ with $H^4(N_{\mathbb H})$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:ghost-splitting}
Suppose that $k\ge1$ coordinates are indispensable.  Let
$Z_{\mathrm{red}}$ denote the quaternionic moment-angle space obtained
after removing the corresponding ghost vertices.  Then there are
homeomorphisms
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)
\cong
Z_{\mathrm{red}}\times(\mathbb S^{3})^k
\]
and
\[
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)
\cong
Z_{\mathrm{red}}\times(\mathbb S^{3})^{k-1}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
An indispensable coordinate is a ghost vertex of the simplicial complex
and contributes an $\mathbb S^{3}$ factor to the polyhedral product.  Together
with Theorem~\ref{thm:polyprod}, this gives the first homeomorphism.

For the second, write a point in the product model as
\[
(z,g_1,\ldots,g_k).
\]
The diagonal left $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ action can be gauged by the first factor:
\[
[z,g_1,\ldots,g_k]
\longmapsto
\bigl(g_1^{-1}z,\,
g_1^{-1}g_2,\ldots,g_1^{-1}g_k\bigr).
\]
This gives the stated homeomorphism of quotient spaces.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:combinatorial}
Let $\Lambda,\Lambda'\subset\mathbb R^{4m}$ be admissible configurations of
$n$ vectors. Suppose there are a permutation $\sigma$ of $[n]$ and a
homeomorphism $P_\Lambda\to P_{\Lambda'}$ which maps the face
$\{x_i=0\}$ onto the face $\{x'_{\sigma(i)}=0\}$ for every $i$.
Then
\[
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\cong N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda')
\]
as topological manifolds.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
After renumbering the coordinates of $\Lambda'$ by $\sigma$, the given
homeomorphism induces a homeomorphism between the two quotient
models
\[
(\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n\times P)/\sim.
\]
This homeomorphism leaves the quaternionic phase coordinates unchanged and
therefore commutes with the diagonal left $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ action.  Passing to the
diagonal quotient gives the result.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:tangent}
The normal bundle of $N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ in $\mathbb H P^{n-1}$ is trivial and
\[
TN_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\oplus\mathbb R^{4m}
\cong i^\ast T\mathbb H P^{n-1}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The regularity argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:smooth}, after projectivization,
shows that $0$ is a regular value of $f$.  Since the target is the vector
space $\mathbb R^{4m}$, the differential provides a trivialization of the normal
bundle.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:p1}
For every LVMQ manifold,
\[
p_1(TN_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda))=2(n-2)e.
\]
Moreover, $N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ is spin.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
All bundles in the stable identity are oriented, so their
complexifications have first Chern class zero. The Whitney formula for
$c_2$ therefore gives integral additivity of $p_1=-c_2$ of the
complexification. Hence
$p_1(TN_{\mathbb H})=n(2e)-4e=2(n-2)e$.
Since $N_{\mathbb H}$ is $2$-connected,
$H^2(N_{\mathbb H};\mathbb Z/2)=0$, so $w_2=0$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
If there are no indispensable coordinates, then
\[
\frac{p_1}{2}=(n-2)e\neq0.
\]
Consequently these LVMQ manifolds are not string manifolds; for a spin
manifold the string obstruction is the class $p_1/2\in H^4(-;\mathbb Z)$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:H4}, $e$ generates an infinite cyclic group, and
$n>4m\geq4$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:minimal}
In this case
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\cong(\mathbb S^{3})^n,
\qquad
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\cong(\mathbb S^{3})^{n-1}=(\mathbb S^{3})^{4m}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Only the quaternionic phases vary in $Z_{\mathbb H}$.  Quotienting by the diagonal
left $\mathbb S^{3}$ action allows one to normalize one of these phases.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:simplex-realization}
Let $p=4m$ and $d\ge1$.  In $\mathbb R^p$ take
\[
\lambda_j=e_j\quad(1\le j\le p),
\qquad
\lambda_{p+\ell}=-(1,\ldots,1)
\quad(1\le\ell\le d+1).
\]
Then the configuration is admissible, the first $p$ coordinates are
precisely the indispensable ones, and its associated polytope is affinely
isomorphic to $\Delta^d$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Write the polytope coordinates as
$(x_1,\ldots,x_p,y_1,\ldots,y_{d+1})$.  The weight equations are
\[
x_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^{d+1}y_\ell=:S
\qquad(1\le j\le p),
\]
and the normalization gives $(p+1)S=1$.  Hence
\[
x_j=\frac1{p+1},
\qquad
 y_\ell\ge0,
\qquad
\sum_{\ell=1}^{d+1}y_\ell=\frac1{p+1}.
\]
Thus $P_\Lambda$ is a scaled $d$-simplex, and the first $p$ coordinates
are positive everywhere.  Since $d\ge1$, omitting any one of the last
$d+1$ vectors still leaves at least one copy of $-(1,\ldots,1)$, so those
coordinates are not indispensable.

Finally, if the origin lies in the convex hull of a subconfiguration,
that subconfiguration must contain at least one negative vector.  If the
total coefficient of the negative vectors is $B>0$, the $j$th coordinate
equation forces the coefficient of every $e_j$ to equal $B$.  Hence all
$p$ positive basis vectors and at least one negative vector occur, so the
subconfiguration has at least $p+1$ elements.  This is weak hyperbolicity,
and the displayed convex relation also proves the Siegel condition.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:einstein-family}
For every $m\ge1$ and every $d\ge1$ there are admissible configurations
for which
\[
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)
\cong
\mathbb S^{4d+3}\times(\mathbb S^{3})^{4m-1}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Use the configuration of Lemma~\ref{lem:simplex-realization}, with
$p=4m$.  Its equations give
\[
|q_j|^2=\frac1{p+1}\qquad(1\le j\le p)
\]
and
\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^{d+1}|q_{p+\ell}|^2=\frac1{p+1}.
\]
Hence, after a constant rescaling of the factors,
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)
\cong
\mathbb S^{4d+3}\times(\mathbb S^3)^p
\]
as smooth manifolds.  The diagonal left $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ action is
\[
a\cdot(z,g_1,\ldots,g_p)
=
(az,ag_1,\ldots,ag_p).
\]
Since $p=4m\ge1$, use the first $\mathbb S^3$ factor as a global gauge:
\[
[z,g_1,\ldots,g_p]
\longmapsto
\bigl(g_1^{-1}z,\,
g_1^{-1}g_2,\ldots,g_1^{-1}g_p\bigr).
\]
This is a smooth diffeomorphism
\[
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)
\cong
\mathbb S^{4d+3}\times(\mathbb S^3)^{p-1}
=
\mathbb S^{4d+3}\times(\mathbb S^3)^{4m-1}.
\]
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:homogeneous-einstein-family}
Every manifold in Theorem~\ref{thm:einstein-family} admits a homogeneous
Einstein metric of positive scalar curvature.  Hence there are infinitely
many nonminimal LVMQ manifolds with positive Einstein metrics.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Give the sphere factors their standard round metrics.  If $\rho_1$ is
the radius of $\mathbb S^{4d+3}$ and $\rho_2$ is the common radius of the
$\mathbb S^3$ factors, then
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathbb S^{4d+3}(\rho_1)}
=
\frac{4d+2}{\rho_1^2}g_1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathbb S^3(\rho_2)}
=
\frac{2}{\rho_2^2}g_2.
\]
Choose
\[
\rho_1^2=(2d+1)\rho_2^2.
\]
All factors then have the same Einstein constant, so their Riemannian
product is Einstein.  The metric is homogeneous under
\[
SO(4d+4)\times SO(4)^{\,4m-1}.
\]
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The corollary concerns the standard homogeneous product metric on the
displayed product of spheres.  It does not assert that the metric obtained
by Riemannian submersion from the original quadratic realization is
Einstein.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:nosymp}
A positive-dimensional compact LVMQ manifold admits no symplectic form.
Consequently it admits no K\"ahler or hyperk\"ahler metric.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:2connN},
\[
H^2(N_{\mathbb H};\mathbb R)=0.
\]
If $\omega$ were symplectic, then $[\omega]\neq0$, since a top power of
$\omega$ is a volume form on the compact manifold.  This is impossible.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:no-QK}
No positive-dimensional LVMQ manifold admits a quaternionic K\"ahler
metric.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Write
\[
\dim N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)=4r.
\]
In our range $m\ge1$ and $n\ge4m+1$, so $r\ge3$; in particular we are
above real dimension four.

We separate two cases.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 1: there is at least one indispensable coordinate.}
Let $k\ge1$ be the number of indispensable coordinates.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:ghost-splitting},
\[
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)
\cong
Z_{\mathrm{red}}\times(\mathbb S^{3})^{k-1},
\]
where $Z_{\mathrm{red}}$ has no indispensable coordinates.
The generalized Hochster formula gives
\[
H^4(Z_{\mathrm{red}};\mathbb R)=0,
\]
and the K\"unneth theorem therefore gives
\[
H^4(N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda);\mathbb R)=0.
\]
A quaternionic K\"ahler manifold of dimension at least eight carries a
parallel fundamental $4$-form $\Omega$ whose top power is a nonzero
multiple of the Riemannian volume form \cite{Salamon}.  Hence
\[
[\Omega]\neq0\in H^4(N_{\mathbb H};\mathbb R),
\]
a contradiction.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 2: there are no indispensable coordinates.}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:H4},
\[
H^4(N_{\mathbb H};\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z e.
\]
Let
\[
i:N_{\mathbb H}\hookrightarrow\mathbb H P^{n-1}
\]
be the natural embedding and let
$u\in H^4(\mathbb H P^{n-1};\mathbb Z)$ be the Euler class of the Hopf bundle with the orientation chosen above,
so that
\[
e=i^\ast u.
\]

The manifold $N_{\mathbb H}$ is the regular zero set of the globally defined
map
\[
f:\mathbb H P^{n-1}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{4m}.
\]
Equivalently, it is the zero set of a transverse section of the trivial
oriented bundle
\[
\mathbb H P^{n-1}\times\mathbb R^{4m}.
\]
Its Poincar\'e dual in $\mathbb H P^{n-1}$ is therefore the Euler class of a
trivial positive-rank bundle, hence zero:
\[
\operatorname{PD}_{\mathbb H P^{n-1}}[N_{\mathbb H}]=0.
\]
Consequently
\[
\left\langle e^r,[N_{\mathbb H}]\right\rangle
=
\left\langle
u^r\smile\operatorname{PD}[N_{\mathbb H}],
[\mathbb H P^{n-1}]
\right\rangle
=0.
\]
Since $H^{4r}(N_{\mathbb H};\mathbb R)$ is one-dimensional, this means
\[
e^r=0.
\]

If a quaternionic K\"ahler metric existed, its parallel fundamental
$4$-form would satisfy
\[
[\Omega]=c\,e
\]
for some real number $c$, because $H^4(N_{\mathbb H};\mathbb R)$ is
one-dimensional.  But then
\[
[\Omega]^r=c^r e^r=0,
\]
whereas $\Omega^r$ is a nonzero multiple of the volume form.  This is
again a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
The homogeneous Einstein metrics of
Corollary~\ref{cor:homogeneous-einstein-family} are not quaternionic
K\"ahler.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:no-compatible-3sasakian}
The manifold $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ admits no $3$-Sasakian structure whose
Reeb $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ action is the diagonal action defining
$N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Such a structure would induce a quaternionic K\"ahler metric on
$N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$, contrary to Theorem~\ref{thm:no-QK}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:commuting}
One has
\[
[V_r,V_s](q)_\alpha=
q_\alpha[\lambda_\alpha^r,\lambda_\alpha^s].
\]
Therefore the fields commute if and only if, for each fixed $\alpha$,
\[
[\lambda_\alpha^r,\lambda_\alpha^s]=0
\]
for all $r,s$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:fixedslice}
In the fixed-slice case,
\[
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\cong Z_{\mathbb C}(\widetilde\Lambda).
\]
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:wall}
Across a generic wall-crossing of type $(a,b)$, the associated simple
polytope changes by a flip of type $(a,b)$.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
This is the standard Gale-duality wall-crossing argument for intersections
of real quadrics; see Bosio--Meersseman \cite{BM}.  At a generic crossing
exactly one affine dependence changes sign.  In the Gale dual this replaces
the corresponding face by its complementary face, which is precisely a
flip of type $(a,b)$.  The argument uses only the oriented real
configuration in $\mathbb R^{4m}$ and therefore is unchanged by the use of
quaternionic coordinates.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:kraines-imaginary}
For $s\ge2$, the restriction of $\Omega_{\mathrm K}$ to
\[
(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^s\subset\mathbb H^s
\]
is nondegenerate in the $4$-plectic sense.  More generally, for every
$t\ge0$ its restriction to
\[
(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^s\oplus\mathbb H^t
\]
is nondegenerate.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
On $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H\simeq\mathbb R^3$, the three numbers
\[
\bigl(\omega_1(x,y),\omega_2(x,y),\omega_3(x,y)\bigr)
\]
are, up to a fixed choice of orientation and signs, the coordinates of
$x\times y$.

Let $0\ne x=(x_1,\ldots,x_s)\in(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^s$, and after
reordering suppose that $x_1\ne0$.  Choose $y$ supported in the first
summand so that $x_1\times y_1\ne0$.  Since $s\ge2$, choose $z,w$
supported in the second summand so that $z_2\times w_2$ is a nonzero
multiple of $x_1\times y_1$.  The mixed two-form terms vanish because
the two pairs have disjoint supports, and therefore
\[
\Omega_{\mathrm K}(x,y,z,w)
=
2\langle x_1\times y_1,z_2\times w_2\rangle\ne0.
\]
Thus $\iota_x\Omega_{\mathrm K}\ne0$.

For $(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^s\oplus\mathbb H^t$, if the imaginary component
of a nonzero vector is nonzero, use the preceding argument with the
other three vectors in $(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^s$.  If its imaginary
component is zero, use the nondegeneracy of the standard Kraines form
on the quaternionic summand $\mathbb H^t$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:lvmq-quaternionic-toric}
For every $m\ge1$ and $d\ge1$, the LVMQ manifolds of
Theorem~\ref{thm:einstein-family},
\[
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)
\cong
\mathbb S^{4d+3}\times(\mathbb S^3)^{4m-1},
\]
are quaternionic toric manifolds in the sense of
Gentili--Gori--Sarfatti \cite{GGS}.  A $4$-plectic form is given by the
restriction of the Kraines form of $\mathbb H P^{n-1}$.

The minimal examples
\[
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\cong(\mathbb S^3)^{4m}
\]
have the same property.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Use the explicit configuration of Lemma~\ref{lem:simplex-realization}
and put $p=4m$, so that $n=p+d+1$.  At a convenient point of
$Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$, the first $p$ coordinates are positive real numbers
of fixed modulus, while in the last block only one coordinate is
nonzero.  The first $p$ fixed-radius factors contribute
$(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^p$, and the tangent space to the sphere in the
last block contributes
\[
\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H\oplus\mathbb H^d.
\]
The vertical tangent space of the diagonal left $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ action is one
weighted diagonal copy of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$.  A real orthogonal
change among these $p+1$ quaternionic coordinate slots sends that
weighted diagonal to the last coordinate axis; because the coefficients
are real, it is quaternionic linear and preserves $\Omega_{\mathrm K}$.
Hence the horizontal tangent space of the quotient is equivalent to
\[
(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^p\oplus\mathbb H^d
=
(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^{4m}\oplus\mathbb H^d.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:kraines-imaginary}, the restriction of the Kraines
form has trivial contraction kernel there.

Let $\operatorname{Sp}(1)^p$ act by right multiplication on the first $p$
coordinates, and let $\operatorname{Sp}(d+1)$ act on the last $d+1$ coordinates,
written as a row vector, by $q\mapsto qB$ with $BB^\ast=I$. The group
\[
\operatorname{Sp}(1)^p\times\operatorname{Sp}(d+1)
\]
acts transitively on the corresponding product model of
$Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$, preserves the defining equations, commutes with the
diagonal left $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ action, and preserves the ambient quaternionic
projective metric and its Kraines form.  The preceding calculation
therefore holds at every point of $N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$.  Since the
Kraines form is closed, its restriction is $4$-plectic.

Put
\[
r=\frac14\dim N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)=d+3m.
\]
Choose $r$ coordinate factors of the right $\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n$ action and denote
their product by $G\cong\operatorname{Sp}(1)^r$.  There remain
\[
n-r=m+1
\]
unselected coordinates.  On the open dense stratum where all
coordinates are nonzero, suppose that $u\in G$ fixes $[q]$.  Then there
is $a\in\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ such that
\[
a q_i=q_i u_i
\]
on selected coordinates and $a q_j=q_j$ on unselected coordinates.
Since an unselected coordinate is nonzero, $a=1$, and then all
$u_i=1$.  Thus the principal isotropy is trivial, and the action is
effective.

The restricted Kraines form $\Omega$ is invariant under $G$.
The sphere-product description gives $H^4(N_{\mathbb H};\mathbb R)=0$, so
$\Omega=d\beta$ for a $3$-form $\beta$. Averaging $\beta$ over the
compact group $G$ gives an invariant primitive, still denoted by
$\beta$. For every fundamental field $Y$, Cartan's formula gives
\[
\iota_Y\Omega=\iota_Yd\beta=-d(\iota_Y\beta).
\]
Thus the action is generalized Hamiltonian in the sense of
\cite[Definition~2.2]{GGS}.

For an
$\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ factor with infinitesimal generators $X_1,X_2,X_3$, the
one-form
\[
\iota_{X_3}\iota_{X_2}\iota_{X_1}\Omega
\]
is closed.  Indeed, the $3$-vector
$X_1\wedge X_2\wedge X_3$ has zero Lie algebra boundary:
$[X_1,X_2]\wedge X_3-[X_1,X_3]\wedge X_2+
[X_2,X_3]\wedge X_1=0$. Each term vanishes because each bracket
is a multiple of the remaining generator. Cartan's formula, together
with invariance and $d\Omega=0$, then gives closedness.  Since every LVMQ manifold
is $2$-connected, $H^1(N_{\mathbb H};\mathbb R)=0$.  Hence these closed one-forms
are exact, and their primitives give the tri-moment map.  Averaging these primitives over $G$ makes the tri-moment map
invariant; this is also \cite[Proposition~2.4]{GGS}.
Therefore $N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ is quaternionic toric.

In the minimal case the same tangent-space calculation leaves
$(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H)^{4m}$ after quotienting the diagonal
$\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:kraines-imaginary} again gives
$4$-plectic nondegeneracy, and the same symmetry and tri-moment
argument applies.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The polytope $P_\Lambda$ is not the tri-moment polytope of this
quaternionic toric action.  Indeed,
\[
\dim P_\Lambda=n-4m-1,
\qquad
\frac14\dim N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)=n-m-1,
\]
and these dimensions differ for $m\ge1$.  Thus the LVM orbit polytope
and the polyhedral data of the quaternionic toric structure play
different roles.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
Determine which general admissible configurations $\Lambda$, beyond the
sphere-product family of Theorem~\ref{thm:lvmq-quaternionic-toric}, admit
a quaternionic toric structure compatible with a subgroup of the
coordinatewise $\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n$ action, and describe the corresponding
tri-moment data.
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- problem-2: body_md -->
Relate the Euler class
\[
e=i^\ast u
\]
of the diagonal Hopf bundle to the Euler class occurring in the
classification of local quaternionic toric actions.
<!-- end problem-2 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:poincare-orbits}
Let $q\in E_I^\ast$.  The isotropy subgroup of $q$ for the action
\eqref{eq:poincare-action} is the vector subspace $K_I$.  Consequently
the ambient orbit through $q$ is naturally diffeomorphic to
\[
\mathbb R^p/K_I\cong\mathbb R^{\varrho(I)}.
\]
In particular its dimension depends only on the support.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Since $q_i\neq0$ for $i\in I$, the equality
$\Phi_T(q)=q$ is equivalent to
\[
e^{\langle\lambda_i,T\rangle}=1
\qquad(i\in I).
\]
The exponent is real, so this is equivalent to
\[
\langle\lambda_i,T\rangle=0
\qquad(i\in I).
\]
Thus the isotropy is exactly $K_I$.  The remaining statements follow
from the rank theorem.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:no-arithmetic}
Since the exponents are real, the isotropy $K_I$ is a vector subspace
and has no discrete part. Every ambient leaf through a nonzero point is
diffeomorphic to a Euclidean space.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The quaternionic configuration $\Lambda$ lies in the
\emph{Poincar\'e domain} if
\[
0\notin\operatorname{conv}\{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\}
\subset\mathbb R^{4m}.
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:q-cone}
Assume that $\Lambda$ lies in the Poincar\'e domain and fix
$\xi\in C_\Lambda$.  Then
\[
\Theta_r:\mathbb S_r^{4n-1}\times\mathbb R
\longrightarrow
\mathbb H^n\setminus\{0\},
\qquad
(q,t)\longmapsto\Phi_{t\xi}(q),
\]
is a diffeomorphism.

Moreover, if $\mathcal F_\Lambda$ denotes the ambient orbit foliation,
then $\Theta_r$ identifies every punctured ambient leaf with the
product of its intersection with $\mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$ and $\mathbb R$.  Thus
$\mathcal F_\Lambda$ on $\mathbb H^n\setminus\{0\}$ is the open cone over its
trace foliation on the sphere.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
For $q\neq0$,
\[
g_q(t)=\|\Phi_{t\xi}(q)\|^2
=
\sum_j|q_j|^2
e^{2t\langle\lambda_j,\xi\rangle}.
\]
By~\eqref{eq:positive-xi},
\[
g_q'(t)
=
2\sum_j
|q_j|^2
e^{2t\langle\lambda_j,\xi\rangle}
\langle\lambda_j,\xi\rangle
>0.
\]
Also
\[
\lim_{t\to-\infty}g_q(t)=0,
\qquad
\lim_{t\to+\infty}g_q(t)=+\infty.
\]
Hence every $\mathbb R\xi$ orbit meets $\mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$ exactly once.
The hitting time depends smoothly on $q$ by the implicit function
theorem, because $g_q'(t)$ never vanishes.  This gives the
diffeomorphism and its inverse.

Since $\mathbb R\xi$ is contained in the acting group, the same
decomposition applies leaf by leaf.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:q-trace-action}
The maps $\Psi_U$, $U\in H_\xi$, define a smooth action of the
additive vector group $H_\xi$ on $\mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$.  Its orbits are exactly
the connected components of the intersections of the nonzero ambient
orbits with the sphere.

If $q\in E_I^\ast\cap \mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$, then the trace leaf through $q$ has
dimension
\[
\varrho(I)-1
\]
and is diffeomorphic to
\[
\mathbb R^{\varrho(I)-1}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Existence and smoothness of $\tau$ follow from the same strict
monotonicity used in Theorem~\ref{thm:q-cone}.  The uniqueness of the
radial correction gives
\[
\Psi_U\circ\Psi_V=\Psi_{U+V},
\]
so this is an action.

The ambient orbit through $q$ is $\mathbb R^{\varrho(I)}$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:poincare-orbits}.  The vector field generated by
$\xi$ is everywhere transverse to the sphere, because
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}
\|\Phi_{t\xi}(q)\|^2
=
2\sum_i|q_i|^2\langle\lambda_i,\xi\rangle>0.
\]
Therefore the intersection with the sphere has codimension one inside
the ambient orbit and dimension $\varrho(I)-1$.

The trace isotropy is a vector subspace of $H_\xi$.  Hence the trace
leaf is a quotient of a real vector space by a vector subspace, and is
therefore diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^{\varrho(I)-1}$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:qtrace-singular}
The trace decomposition on $\mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$ is a
Stefan--Sussmann singular foliation.  On the stratum
$E_I^\ast\cap \mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$ it is regular of dimension $\varrho(I)-1$.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:qgeneric-trace}
Under~\eqref{eq:qgeneric}, if $|I|=s$, then every trace leaf in
$E_I^\ast\cap \mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$ is diffeomorphic to
\[
\begin{cases}
\mathbb R^{s-1},&s\le p,\\[2mm]
\mathbb R^{p-1},&s\ge p.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular, if $n\ge4m$, the principal trace leaves are all
$\mathbb R^{4m-1}$.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:q-stratum-quotient}
For every support $I$, the ambient orbit space on the coordinate
stratum is naturally a smooth manifold
\[
E_I^\ast/\mathbb R^p
\cong
\mathbb R^s/A_I(\mathbb R^p)\times(\mathbb S^{3})^s
\cong
\mathbb R^{s-\varrho(I)}\times(\mathbb S^{3})^s.
\]
By the conical model, the same space is the leaf space of the trace
foliation on $E_I^\ast\cap \mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$:
\[
\bigl(E_I^\ast\cap \mathbb S_r^{4n-1}\bigr)/
\widehat{\mathcal F}_\Lambda
\cong
\mathbb R^{s-\varrho(I)}\times(\mathbb S^{3})^s.
\]
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The first statement follows from the logarithmic radial coordinates:
the action translates the $\mathbb R^s$ factor by the closed vector subspace
$A_I(\mathbb R^p)$ and leaves all quaternionic phases fixed.  The quotient is
therefore
\[
\mathbb R^s/A_I(\mathbb R^p)\times(\mathbb S^{3})^s.
\]
The second statement follows because
Theorem~\ref{thm:q-cone} identifies every punctured ambient leaf with a
trace leaf times $\mathbb R$ and therefore identifies the two leaf spaces.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:q-support}
Let $q\in \mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$ and let $y$ belong to the closure of its trace
leaf.  Then
\[
I(y)\subseteq I(q).
\]
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
If $q_j=0$, then the $j$th coordinate remains zero under the ambient
action and under the radial correction.  The same is true on the
closure.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:no-recurrence}
A trace leaf is closed inside its support stratum
\[
E_I^\ast\cap \mathbb S_r^{4n-1}.
\]
Consequently every limit point of a trace leaf which is not on the leaf
itself has strictly smaller support.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
In logarithmic radial coordinates on $E_I^\ast$, an ambient orbit is
an affine translate of the closed vector subspace $A_I(\mathbb R^p)$,
together with a fixed point of $(\mathbb S^{3})^s$.  Hence it is closed in
$E_I^\ast$.  Its intersection with the sphere is therefore closed in
$E_I^\ast\cap \mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$.  The second assertion follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:q-support}.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:q-phase-transverse}
The group $\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n$ acts by automorphisms of the trace foliation.
On each support stratum, the quotient description of
Theorem~\ref{thm:q-stratum-quotient} is equivariant with respect to
the natural $\operatorname{Sp}(1)^I$ action on the factor $(\mathbb S^{3})^I$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:q-qc-isotropic}
Every trace leaf of the Poincar\'e foliation is tangent to
$\mathcal H$.  Moreover, for every $\alpha=1,2,3$,
\[
d\eta_\alpha|_{T\widehat{\mathcal L}}=0.
\]
Equivalently, the tangent space of a trace leaf is simultaneously
isotropic for the three fundamental $2$-forms of the standard
$3$-Sasakian structure.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
A tangent vector to a trace leaf has the form
\[
Y=(c_1q_1,\ldots,c_nq_n),
\qquad c_i\in\mathbb R,
\]
with
\[
\sum_i c_i|q_i|^2=0
\]
because $Y$ is tangent to the sphere.  For every imaginary unit
$I_\alpha$,
\[
\eta_\alpha(Y)
=
\frac1{r^2}
\sum_i c_i\langle q_i,I_\alpha q_i\rangle
=0,
\]
since $\langle q,I_\alpha q\rangle=0$.  Thus
$Y\in\mathcal H$.

Differentiating the definition of $\eta_\alpha$ gives, for horizontal
vectors,
\[
d\eta_\alpha(Y,Z)
=
\frac{2}{r^2}\langle I_\alpha Y,Z\rangle
=
-\frac{2}{r^2}\langle Y,I_\alpha Z\rangle.
\]
If
\[
Y=(c_iq_i),\qquad Z=(d_iq_i)
\]
are tangent to the same trace leaf, then
\[
\langle Y,I_\alpha Z\rangle
=
\sum_i c_id_i\langle q_i,I_\alpha q_i\rangle
=0.
\]
Hence $d\eta_\alpha(Y,Z)=0$ for all $\alpha$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:q-totally-real}
The restriction of $\pi$ to every trace leaf is an isometric immersion
for the submersion metric.  Its image is totally real with respect to the quaternionic structure
of $\mathbb H P^{n-1}$.  If $I_1,I_2,I_3$ is a local quaternionic frame and
$\omega_\alpha(V,W)=g(I_\alpha V,W)$ are the corresponding fundamental
$2$-forms, then
\[
\omega_\alpha|_{d\pi(T\widehat{\mathcal L})}=0,
\qquad \alpha=1,2,3.
\]
In particular the Kraines $4$-form vanishes on four tangent vectors of
a projected trace leaf.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
The Hopf map is a Riemannian submersion on the horizontal distribution.
The horizontal pullbacks of the local fundamental $2$-forms are
multiples of $d\eta_\alpha$.  The assertion follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:q-qc-isotropic}.  The Kraines form is, locally and up
to normalization,
\[
\Omega_{\mathrm K}
=
\omega_1\wedge\omega_1+
\omega_2\wedge\omega_2+
\omega_3\wedge\omega_3,
\]
so its restriction to the projected leaf is zero.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
For the LVMQ range $n>4m$, a principal trace leaf has dimension
$4m-1<n-1$, which is compatible with the usual dimension bound for a
totally real subspace of a quaternionic Hermitian vector space of
quaternionic dimension $n-1$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:q-trace-metric}
For $U,V\in H_\xi$, the round metric of $\mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$ induces on the
trace leaf the bilinear form
\[
g^{\rm tr}_q(U,V)
=
r^2\sum_{i\in I}x_i
\left(\lambda_U(i)-b_i\frac{\bar\lambda_U}{\bar b}\right)
\left(\lambda_V(i)-b_i\frac{\bar\lambda_V}{\bar b}\right),
\]
where $\lambda_U(i)=\langle\lambda_i,U\rangle$.  Its kernel is exactly
the infinitesimal isotropy of the trace action,
\[
\{U\in H_\xi:\ U+c\xi\in K_I\text{ for some }c\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
Consequently it is positive definite on the tangent space of the trace
leaf, whose dimension is $\varrho(I)-1$.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Differentiate the norm constraint for
$\Phi_{U+\tau(U,q)\xi}(q)$.  At the given point this gives
\[
0=2\sum_i x_i\bigl(\lambda_U(i)+\dot\tau_U b_i\bigr),
\]
which is the displayed formula for $\dot\tau_U$.  Since
$q_i=r\sqrt{x_i}u_i$ with fixed phases, the radial part of the round
metric is
\[
ds^2=\frac{r^2}{4}\sum_i\frac{dx_i^2}{x_i}.
\]
Moreover
\[
d\log x_i[U]
=2\left(\lambda_U(i)-b_i\frac{\bar\lambda_U}{\bar b}\right).
\]
Substitution gives the metric formula.

The quadratic form vanishes exactly when
$\lambda_U(i)=c b_i$ for all $i\in I$, where
$c=\bar\lambda_U/\bar b$.  Equivalently
$U-c\xi\in K_I$, which is precisely the infinitesimal isotropy of the
trace action.  The dimension statement agrees with
Theorem~\ref{thm:q-trace-action}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:q-hessian-normalized}
The metric induced on the radially normalized orbit is
\[
g_T^{\rm norm}(U,V)
=
r^2\operatorname{Cov}_{x(T)}(\lambda_U,\lambda_V)
=
\frac{r^2}{4}D^2\varphi_T(U,V).
\]
Its kernel is exactly $K_I^{\rm norm}$, so it is positive definite on
$\mathbb R^p/K_I^{\rm norm}$.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Along~\eqref{eq:exp-family},
\[
d\log x_i(T)[U]
=2\left(\lambda_U(i)-\sum_jx_j(T)\lambda_U(j)\right).
\]
Substitution into
$ds^2=(r^2/4)\sum_i dx_i^2/x_i$ gives the covariance formula, and direct
differentiation of $\varphi$ gives the Hessian formula.  A weighted
variance vanishes exactly when the values $\lambda_U(i)$ are constant on
$I$, which is the stated kernel.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The normalized orbit in Proposition~\ref{prop:q-hessian-normalized} need
not coincide with the trace leaf, because radial normalization by a common
scalar need not be generated by the real weight action.  They coincide on
the support $I$ if there exists $R\in\mathbb R^p$ such that
$\langle\lambda_i,R\rangle=1$ for every $i\in I$; in that special case a
common radial rescaling is an action direction and the Hessian metric
restricts to the trace leaf after quotienting that direction.  No such
assumption is made in general.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:q-not-basic}
Let $Y$ be a nonvanishing local leafwise vector field tangent to a trace
leaf.  Then, for each $\alpha$, there is a horizontal vector $Z$ with
$d\eta_\alpha(Y,Z)\neq0$. Consequently $\mathcal L_Y\eta_\alpha$
restricted to $\mathcal H$ is not zero, so $\mathcal L_Y\eta_\alpha$
does not belong to the span of $\eta_1,\eta_2,\eta_3$ over the smooth
functions, and the flow of $Y$ does not preserve $\mathcal H$.
Therefore the standard quaternionic contact structure does not descend
to the local trace leaf space on any regular region with
positive-dimensional leaves.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Since $Y$ is horizontal, so is $I_\alpha Y$.  Taking
$Z=I_\alpha Y$ and differentiating $\eta_\alpha$,
\[
d\eta_\alpha(Y,Z)
=
\frac{2}{r^2}
\langle I_\alpha Y,I_\alpha Y\rangle
=
\frac{2}{r^2}|Y|^2\neq0.
\]
The identity $\iota_Y\eta_\alpha=0$ holds identically for a local
leafwise vector field $Y$, so Cartan's formula gives
$\mathcal L_Y\eta_\alpha=\iota_Yd\eta_\alpha$, whose value on $Z$ is
nonzero. Every function combination of $\eta_1,\eta_2,\eta_3$ vanishes
on $\mathcal H$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:q-noautomatic}
On any open region where the Poincar\'e trace foliation is regular
and has positive-dimensional leaves, the standard quaternionic contact
structure of $\mathbb S^{4n-1}$ does not descend to the local leaf space.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- problem-3: body_md -->
Determine whether the regular principal leaf space
\[
\mathbb R^{n-4m}\times(\mathbb S^{3})^n
\]
admits a natural $4$-plectic form constructed from the weight
configuration and the quaternionic phase factors, and determine
whether such a form can be extended compatibly across the lower
support strata.
<!-- end problem-3 -->
<!-- problem-4: body_md -->
Study the projected trace leaves in $\mathbb H P^{n-1}$ as totally real
submanifolds.  In particular, determine their second fundamental form,
minimality properties, and the configurations for which some of these
leaves are totally geodesic or minimal.
<!-- end problem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:hopf-trace}
On $\mathbb H^n\setminus\{0\}$ the distribution
\[
\mathcal D_R(q)=q\mathbb H
\]
is integrable.  Its leaves are the punctured right quaternionic lines
$q\mathbb H^\ast$.  Their intersections with $\mathbb S^{4n-1}$ are
\[
q\operatorname{Sp}(1)\cong \mathbb S^{3}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\mathbb S^{3}\longrightarrow \mathbb S^{4n-1}\longrightarrow\mathbb H P^{n-1}
\]
is exactly the trace foliation.  It is regular on the sphere; there are
no singular spherical leaves.  In $\mathbb H^n$ the origin is the unique
singular leaf.
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Right multiplication by $\mathbb H^\ast$ is a free action on
$\mathbb H^n\setminus\{0\}$, and its orbits are the punctured right
quaternionic lines.  Restriction to the unit sphere replaces
$\mathbb H^\ast\simeq\mathbb R_{>0}\times\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ by $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$, giving the standard
quaternionic Hopf fibration.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:cyclic-hopf-quotient}
For every $n\ge1$ and every $0<\rho<1$,
\[
(\mathbb H^n\setminus\{0\})/\langle\gamma_\rho\rangle
\cong
\mathbb S^{4n-1}\times \mathbb S^1 .
\]
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Write $q=r u$ with $r>0$ and $u\in\mathbb S^{4n-1}$.  Under the logarithmic
coordinate $t=\log r$, the generator acts by
\[
(u,t)\longmapsto (u,t+\log\rho).
\]
Thus the quotient is
\[
\mathbb S^{4n-1}\times
\bigl(\mathbb R/(\log\rho)\mathbb Z\bigr)
\cong
\mathbb S^{4n-1}\times\mathbb S^1 .
\]
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- theorem-21: body_md -->
\label{thm:linear-frobenius-rigidity}
Let
\[
X(q)=Aq,\qquad A\in GL(n,\mathbb H),\qquad n\ge2,
\]
and let $\mathcal D_X(q)=Aq\,\mathbb H$.  Then $\mathcal D_X$ is involutive on
$\mathbb H^n\setminus\{0\}$ if and only if
\[
A=\mu I,
\qquad \mu\in\mathbb R^\ast.
\]
Hence every right-$\mathbb H$-linear isolated-singularity model with an
involutive quaternionic rank-one distribution has on $\mathbb S^{4n-1}$
exactly the Hopf foliation by $\mathbb S^{3}$'s.
<!-- end theorem-21 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
For $a\in\mathbb H$ put $X_a(q)=Aq\,a$.  Since $A$ is right-$\mathbb H$-linear,
\[
[X_a,X_b](q)=A^2q\,(ab-ba)
\]
for the convention $[V,W]=DW(V)-DV(W)$.  Frobenius integrability
therefore implies
\[
A^2q\,c\in Aq\,\mathbb H
\]
for every $q$ and every purely imaginary quaternion $c$ which occurs as
a commutator.  Choose one nonzero such $c$.  Since both $A$ and $c$ are
invertible, putting $p=Aq$ gives
\[
Ap\in p\mathbb H
\qquad\text{for every }p\neq0.
\]
Thus $A$ preserves every right quaternionic line.

Write
\[
Ae_r=e_r\alpha_r
\]
for the standard basis.  Applying the preceding property to $e_r+e_s$
shows that $\alpha_r=\alpha_s$ for all $r,s$; let their common value be
$\alpha$.  Applying it to $e_1+e_2h$, with arbitrary $h\in\mathbb H$, gives
\[
\alpha h=h\alpha
\qquad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb H.
\]
Therefore $\alpha$ belongs to the center of $\mathbb H$, namely $\mathbb R$, and
$A=\mu I$.  Conversely, for $A=\mu I$ the distribution is $q\mathbb H$ and
is the orbit distribution of right multiplication by $\mathbb H^\ast$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:multi-frobenius}
On a constant-rank stratum, the distribution
\[
\mathcal D(q)
=
\sum_{\alpha=1}^k A_\alpha q\,\mathbb H
\]
is involutive if and only if, for every $\alpha,\beta$, every
$a,b\in\mathbb H$, and every $q$ in that stratum,
\[
A_\beta A_\alpha q\,(ab)
-
A_\alpha A_\beta q\,(ba)
\in
\sum_{\gamma=1}^k A_\gamma q\,\mathbb H.
\]
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
The fields $X_{\alpha,a}$ span $\mathcal D$ over $\mathbb R$.  Frobenius'
criterion is therefore exactly the requirement that all their pairwise
brackets lie in the same distribution.  The displayed bracket formula
gives the stated condition.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{prop:multi-invertible-obstruction}
Assume $k\ge2$. Then there is $q\neq0$ for which
\[
\{A_1q,\ldots,A_kq\}
\]
has right quaternionic rank at most $k-1$.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
If some $A_\alpha$ is singular, take $q\ne0$ with $A_\alpha q=0$.
Otherwise $A_1$ is invertible; set
\[
B_\alpha=A_\alpha A_1^{-1}.
\]
Then $B_1=I$.  Every quaternionic matrix has a right eigenvalue; see
\cite{ZhangQuaternionMatrices}.  Hence there exist $p\neq0$ and
$\lambda\in\mathbb H$ such that
\[
B_2p=p\lambda.
\]
With $q=A_1^{-1}p$ one obtains
\[
A_2q=A_1q\,\lambda.
\]
Thus the first two vectors in
$\{A_1q,\ldots,A_kq\}$ are right-$\mathbb H$-linearly dependent, and the
quaternionic rank is at most $k-1$ at that point.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- problem-5: body_md -->
For $k\ge2$, classify nonlinear families $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ for which
\[
\mathcal D=X_1\mathbb H+\cdots+X_k\mathbb H
\]
has constant rank $4k$ on a punctured neighborhood, is involutive, and
contains a direction transverse to sufficiently small centered spheres.
Describe the induced $(4k-1)$-dimensional trace foliation and its leaf
space.  Determine which additional hypotheses, if any, force compact
leaves or a fibration.
<!-- end problem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:flat-quaternionic}
Every connected $C^2$ quaternionic submanifold of $\mathbb H^n$ has zero
second fundamental form. Its image is contained in an affine
quaternionic subspace, and locally it is an open subset of that subspace.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Let $B(u,v)=(\nabla_u v)^\perp$ be the second fundamental form for
the Euclidean connection. The tangent and normal spaces are invariant
under right multiplication by $i,j,k$. Since these multiplications
are parallel, for $a\in\{i,j,k\}$ we have
\[
B(u,va)=B(u,v)a.
\]
Symmetry of $B$ also gives $B(ua,v)=B(u,v)a$. Applying these identities
in the two orders yields
\[
B(ui,vj)=(B(u,v)i)j=B(u,v)k,
\]
whereas
\[
B(ui,vj)=(B(u,v)j)i=-B(u,v)k.
\]
Thus $B=0$. Parallel translation along a path in the submanifold
preserves its tangent space. Euclidean parallel translation is
constant, so connectedness makes this tangent space a fixed
quaternionic subspace $W$. Integration along paths places the image
in one translate of $W$, and the inverse function theorem gives the
local assertion.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- theorem-22: body_md -->
\label{thm:hopf-like-poincare}
Let $X$ be a $C^2$ real vector field near $0\in\mathbb H^n$, $n\ge2$, with
\[
X(0)=0,\qquad DX(0)=\mu I,\qquad \mu>0.
\]
Suppose $\mathcal D_X(q)=X(q)\mathbb H$ is involutive on a punctured
neighborhood of the origin. Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that
\[
\mathcal D_X(q)=q\mathbb H\qquad(0<\|q\|<\varepsilon).
\]
For every $0<r<\varepsilon$, its trace on $\mathbb S_r^{4n-1}$ is exactly
the standard right Hopf foliation. In particular the quotient is the
standard smooth manifold $\mathbb H P^{n-1}$.
<!-- end theorem-22 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Choose $\varepsilon>0$ so small that $X$ is defined on a neighborhood
of the closed ball and
\[
\langle X(q),q\rangle\ge \frac\mu2\|q\|^2,
\qquad 0<\|q\|\le\varepsilon.
\]
This follows from $X(q)=\mu q+O(\|q\|^2)$, and it implies $X(q)\ne0$.
Hence $\mathcal D_X$ has constant real rank four on the punctured ball.
Frobenius' theorem gives integral leaves; each is a quaternionic
submanifold and is contained in an affine quaternionic line by
Lemma~\ref{lem:flat-quaternionic}.

Fix $q$ in the punctured ball and let $\phi_t(q)$ be its trajectory
under $X$. It exists for all $t\le0$ and stays in the ball: the norm
strictly decreases in backward time, and the vector field is defined
on a neighborhood of the closed ball. Uniqueness prevents a nonzero
trajectory from reaching the equilibrium $0$ in finite time. Moreover,
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\|\phi_t(q)\|^2\ge\mu\|\phi_t(q)\|^2
\]
gives
\[
\|\phi_t(q)\|^2\le e^{\mu t}\|q\|^2\qquad(t\le0).
\]
Thus $\phi_t(q)\to0$ as $t\to-\infty$.

The trajectory stays in the integral leaf through $q$, since $X$ is
tangent to that leaf. Its containing affine quaternionic line is
closed in $\mathbb H^n$ and therefore contains $0$. It is consequently the
linear quaternionic line $q\mathbb H$. The leaf has real dimension four,
so its tangent space at $q$ is $q\mathbb H$. This holds at every point of
the punctured ball and proves the stated equality of distributions.

The maximal leaves in the ball are the connected punctured disks
$(q\mathbb H)\cap(B_\varepsilon\setminus\{0\})$. Their intersections with
a centered sphere are the right $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ orbits. The quotient map is
the usual smooth Hopf projection.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The vector field itself can be nonlinear. For example,
$X(q)=q\,a(q)$, where $a$ is $C^2$ and $a(0)=\mu>0$, has
$X(q)\mathbb H=q\mathbb H$ wherever $a(q)\ne0$. The theorem determines the
quaternionic distribution and its leaves, without asserting linear
conjugacy of the one-dimensional flow of $X$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- theorem-23: body_md -->
\label{thm:q-dichotomy}
Let
\[
\Lambda=(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)
\subset\mathbb H^m\simeq\mathbb R^{4m}
\]
be of full affine rank, and let $\Phi$ be the real action
\eqref{eq:poincare-action}.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item If
\[
0\in\operatorname{conv}\Lambda
\]
and the weak hyperbolicity condition holds, then on the Siegel open
set every orbit has a unique point of minimum norm.  The normalized
minimum set is $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$, and
\[
\mathcal S_\Lambda
\cong
Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\times\mathbb R^{4m}\times\mathbb R_{>0}.
\]
After quaternionic projectivization the leaf space is the compact
LVMQ manifold $N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$.

\item If
\[
0\notin\operatorname{conv}\Lambda,
\]
then there exists $\xi\in\mathbb R^{4m}$ for which the norm is strictly
increasing along every $\mathbb R\xi$ orbit.  Every sphere is a global
section for this one-dimensional subaction and
\[
\mathbb H^n\setminus\{0\}
\cong
\mathbb S_r^{4n-1}\times\mathbb R.
\]
The residual action on the sphere defines a singular trace foliation
whose leaf in the support stratum $I$ is $\mathbb R^{\varrho(I)-1}$ and whose
stratum leaf space is
\[
\mathbb R^{|I|-\varrho(I)}\times(\mathbb S^{3})^{|I|}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-23 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{prop:conjugation}
Let $G=\operatorname{Sp}(1)^n$ act on $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ on the right, and let
$\Delta\cong\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ be its diagonal subgroup. Coordinatewise
quaternionic conjugation induces a diffeomorphism
\[
N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)\cong Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)/\Delta.
\]
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
The map $C(q)=(\overline q_1,\ldots,\overline q_n)$ preserves all
coordinate norms, hence preserves $Z_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$. It is a smooth
involution and satisfies
\[
C(aq)=C(q)\,\overline a.
\]
It therefore identifies the left diagonal orbits with the right
diagonal orbits and induces the stated diffeomorphism.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- problem-6: body_md -->
Determine the integral cohomology ring of $N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$ from
$K_{P_\Lambda}$ using this diagonal pullback, including the products
and torsion not determined by the Gysin sequence.
<!-- end problem-6 -->
<!-- problem-7: body_md -->
Determine whether labelled combinatorial equivalence of the associated
simple polytopes, with indispensable coordinates matched, always
determines the diffeomorphism type of the corresponding LVMQ manifolds.
<!-- end problem-7 -->
<!-- problem-8: body_md -->
\label{prob:wall}
Give an explicit diagonal-$\operatorname{Sp}(1)$-equivariant local model for a generic
wall crossing and determine the induced smooth surgery on
$N_{\mathbb H}(\Lambda)$.
<!-- end problem-8 -->
